title: Many readers, or one writer

prereqs.why: The whole problem is written around the difference between &T and &mut T and the rule that governs when each is allowed.
A borrow only makes sense once you know what owning the value means.
You have met C++ references, which borrow without the rule - the comparison is most of the lesson.

statement:
Read `n` and `d`, then `n` integers into a `Vec<i64>`. Write four functions with
these exact signatures and use them in this order:

```rust
fn total(v: &Vec<i64>) -> i64          // shared borrow
fn largest(v: &Vec<i64>) -> i64        // shared borrow
fn add_to_all(v: &mut Vec<i64>, d: i64)  // exclusive borrow, modifies in place
fn push_total(v: &mut Vec<i64>)        // exclusive borrow, appends the total
```

Print:

```
total <sum of the original values>
largest <largest original value>
added <the values after adding d to each>
pushed <the values after appending their own total>
total <the sum now, which has changed twice>
```

If `n` is 0, print just `empty`.

```
input:   4 10          output:  total 10
         1 2 3 4                largest 4
                                added 11 12 13 14
                                pushed 11 12 13 14 50
                                total 100
```

### The rule

At any moment, for any value, Rust allows **either**:

- any number of shared references `&T` - all of which can read, none can write
- exactly one exclusive reference `&mut T` - which can write

and never both at once. The compiler checks it; there is no runtime cost.

The reason is not tidiness. It is that a value nobody else can see cannot change
under you, and a value that cannot change can be read by anyone safely. One rule
eliminates data races *and* iterator invalidation *and* aliasing bugs, all of
which are the same mistake wearing different clothes.

### The error worth provoking on purpose

```rust
let first = &v[0];        // shared borrow of v starts here
v.push(99);               // needs &mut v -- rejected
println!("{}", first);    // ...because the shared borrow is still used here
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `v` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
```

`push` may reallocate, which would leave `first` pointing at freed memory. That
is the dangling-iterator bug from the C++ dynamic-array problem, and Rust makes
it a build failure rather than a sanitizer finding. Write it once, read the
error, then take it out.

### Boundary cases

`n = 0`, which prints `empty` and nothing else. `n = 1`. `d = 0`, so `added`
matches the input. Negative values and a negative `d`. All values equal. Note
that the final `total` is affected twice - once by `add_to_all` and once by the
value `push_total` appended - so it is not simply the original sum plus
something.

### Platform assumptions

`n` is between 0 and 1000, each value and `d` fit in an `i64` with
`|value| <= 10^9`, so the sum cannot overflow 64 bits. Rust panics on integer
overflow in debug builds and wraps in release builds, so this problem keeps the
values far from the edge rather than relying on either - the solution explains
why that distinction exists.
hints: Iterating a shared borrow gives you shared references to the elements: `for x in v` where `v: &Vec<i64>` makes `x` an `&i64`, so you need `*x` to get the number. `for x in v.iter()` is the same thing written out.

To modify in place you need `v.iter_mut()`, which yields `&mut i64`, and then `*x += d` writes through it. `for x in v` on a `&mut Vec` also works - the compiler picks `iter_mut` - but writing it explicitly makes the intent obvious.

`push_total` needs to read the vector and then modify it. Do the read first and store the result in a local: `let t = total(v); v.push(t);`. Writing `v.push(total(v))` tries to hold a shared borrow and an exclusive one at the same time, which is the error the problem is about.
